nameStory: This aquatic plant earned its 'pennywort' name from its round, coin-shaped leaves that look like tiny copper pennies floating on the water's surface. The 'floating' part of its name describes its preferred lifestyle - drifting freely in shallow water rather than being firmly rooted like most plants.
description: Floating marsh pennywort is a small aquatic plant that forms mats of round, penny-sized leaves on the water's surface. The bright green leaves are attached to slender, creeping stems that float or trail through shallow water. This member of the ivy family typically spreads horizontally rather than growing tall, creating carpet-like patches in quiet waterways. Each leaf is roughly the size of a nickel or quarter, with a distinctive shield-like shape.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Round, shield-shaped leaves about the size of a coin, bright green and smooth to the touch with a slightly waxy feel. Each leaf attaches to the stem at its center, not at the edge, giving it a distinctive umbrella-like appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms floating mats or carpets on the water surface, with long, slender stems that feel smooth and somewhat squishy when handled. The plant spreads horizontally rather than growing upward.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or greenish flowers appear in small clusters on short stalks that rise just above the water surface. Individual flowers are so small they're easily overlooked without close inspection.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found in or on water - never on dry land. Prefers shallow, still or slow-moving water where it can form extensive floating colonies.

habitat: Floating marsh pennywort thrives in shallow ponds, quiet stream edges, marshes, and slow-moving waterways throughout New England. It prefers still or gently flowing water where it can establish floating colonies without being swept away. You'll often find it mixed with other aquatic plants like duckweeds and water lilies in nutrient-rich waters.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water temperatures warm, with fresh green leaves emerging and stems starting to spread across the water surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with lush mats of round leaves covering the water. Small white flowers may appear on short stalks above the leaf canopy during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows and some leaves may begin to yellow or brown as temperatures drop, though the plant often remains green well into autumn.
seasonality.winter: Dies back in frozen waters but may persist in areas that don't freeze completely. Look for remnant brown stems at the water's edge.

funFact: Despite being called a 'pennywort,' this floating plant is actually related to English ivy and belongs to the same family - making it a distant aquatic cousin of the ivy climbing up your house!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small, round-leaved aquatic plants like American water-pennywort, but floating marsh pennywort's leaves attach at the center (like an umbrella handle) rather than at the edge. Remember: center attachment means floating pennywort, edge attachment means its landlubbing cousins.
contextualKnowledge: This is an extremely rare plant in New England with only one recorded observation, making it a true botanical treasure if you're lucky enough to spot it. The plant is much more common in warmer regions and may be at the northern edge of its range here.
compareHints: Unlike its pennywort relatives in New England, floating marsh pennywort is the only one that forms true floating mats on open water. American water-pennywort grows in wet soil or shallow water margins with leaves that attach at the leaf edge, while manyflower marshpennywort has leaves that are more deeply lobed and also grows in marshy soil rather than floating freely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American water-pennywort can be distinguished from its relatives by its consistently round leaves and preference for the northeastern climate.
Among New England's water pennyworts, manyflower marshpennywort has the most perfectly circular leaves and the most obvious umbrella-shaped flower clusters.
Among New England's pennyworts, whorled pennywort is the easiest to identify because of its perfectly circular leaves attached at the center.
Unlike American Water-pennywort which has kidney-shaped or lobed leaves, Sibthorp's Pennywort has perfectly round, unlobed leaves.
**[UNCERTAIN]** Compared to its more common cousin American Water-pennywort, this species likely differs in leaf size, flower arrangement, or specific habitat requirements.
